sources.title: Technical Artist Bootcamp: User Experience Design Applied to Technical Art
sources.use: The closest topic match: UX applied to tools made by a technical-art team. Use to motivate considering artists throughout development.
sources.status: Official indexed session description verified; tagged free content. Direct page retrieval failed on retry; full video not watched.

sources.title: The System of Tools: Reducing Frustration in a Daily Workflow
sources.use: Use the workflow-system framing for Maya → export → Unreal → verify. Friction can accumulate between tools as well as inside a panel.
sources.status: Official session description read; free-content listing. Full video not watched; no clip timestamps verified.

sources.title: Technical Artist Bootcamp: Production Values: Improving Quality, Longevity and Scalability
sources.use: PDF pages 32–35 discuss familiar interface conventions, hierarchy, grouping, defaults, and tool flow. A concrete LOD Tools example supports professional relevance.
sources.status: Free PDF text and speaker notes inspected; screenshot assets not extracted. Industry guidance, not a controlled study. Avoid turning fewer clicks into a universal goal.

sources.title: The User Experience of Game Development Tools
sources.use: Foundational game-tool UX preparation. Use as a broader resource after the directly applicable TA sessions.
sources.status: Free presentation surfaced by search; session synopsis reviewed, deck not read in full.

sources.title: Mapping User Stories in Agile
sources.use: Use a short artist journey to connect individual tasks to the overall workflow. A story map is larger than one role–goal–benefit sentence.
sources.status: Free article read. Teach only the small task-framing portion here; no Agile process prerequisite.

sources.title: Accounting for UX Work with User Stories in Agile Projects
sources.use: Useful instructor background for attaching usability criteria to a story.
sources.status: Free article reviewed through search extract. Do not turn this into sprint-management instruction.

sources.title: Paper Prototyping: Getting User Data Before You Code
sources.use: Test a sketched interface before implementation. Let the participant indicate actions and have a facilitator supply the next paper state.
sources.status: Free article read. Paper can reveal interpretation and flow issues; it cannot establish Unreal correctness or runtime performance.

sources.title: Usability Testing 101
sources.use: Use a realistic goal, observe the attempt, and record assistance. Distinguish what people do from their opinions about the design.
sources.status: Free article read. Student peer reviews are formative evidence, not representative validation of a professional tool.

sources.title: Parallel & Iterative Design
sources.use: Useful diagrams distinguish exploring alternatives from refining successive versions.
sources.status: Free article reviewed. Do not project its historical improvement percentages onto this class or Unreal tools.

sources.title: Mental Models
sources.use: People predict behavior using what they believe about a system. Ask what an artist expects before revealing the result.
sources.status: Free article read; professional synthesis, not an Unreal experiment.

sources.title: Memory Recognition and Recall in User Interfaces
sources.use: Visible options, paths, and examples can reduce the need to remember syntax or hidden state.
sources.status: Free guidance reviewed. Recognition does not imply showing every advanced setting simultaneously.

sources.title: Parallel Prototyping Leads to Better Design Results, More Divergence, and Increased Self-Efficacy
sources.use: A study of 33 participants designing web advertisements compared parallel and serial prototyping with equal time and feedback. The parallel condition performed better on the reported design outcomes. Teaching inference: compare a few layout alternatives before polishing one.
sources.status: Free author manuscript; methods, results, and discussion inspected. Participants were not professional designers; task was ad design, not editor-tool usability. No numerical gain transferred to Unreal.

sources.title: Beyond the five-user assumption: Benefits of increased sample sizes in usability testing
sources.use: The published abstract reports substantial variation in problems found by five-person samples drawn from 60 users. Small tests can help without guaranteeing that all important problems have been found.
sources.status: Free abstract only; full publisher article paywalled. Not required reading or a free full-paper recommendation.

sources.title: Principles of great design
sources.use: Useful chapters: agency 1:52, familiarity 6:04, simplicity 11:13. Transfer control, familiar behavior, and clear hierarchy to artist tools.
sources.status: Official transcript and chapter list read; video not watched end to end. These are design recommendations, not experimental proof.

sources.title: Essential Design Principles
sources.use: Mental-model explanation around 29:36–32:00. Use expectations to discuss why a familiar-looking control can still surprise a user.
sources.status: Official transcript excerpt verified; useful targeted segment, not a recommendation to watch the whole talk first.

sources.title: Feedback · Human Interface Guidelines
sources.use: Match interruption to consequence: routine status can stay near the work; significant, actionable risks can warrant interruption.
sources.status: Free guidance read. Adapt the principle to Unreal conventions; do not imitate Apple styling or assume all confirmations are helpful.

sources.title: Create and manage prototype flows
sources.use: Connected frames let an instructor demonstrate a starting state, action, and result. The documented flow feature is available on all plans and requires edit access.
sources.status: Official help read. A Figma file/account may be needed to author; no student account or installation required for this lesson.

topics.title: Describe the artist’s goal before designing the panel
topics.placement: Proposed insertion after 14; before scope/layout examples.
copy: What are they trying to accomplish—and why?
topics.example: As an environment artist, I want to bring a revised prop from Maya into Unreal so I can inspect it in the level without rebuilding its setup. This is an illustrative story, not a verified user requirement.
topics.notes: A user story helps us discuss the job this tool should support. It is not a request for a particular button. Ask what the artist is doing now and where the difficulty occurs. Then turn the goal into things we can observe: the intended asset is updated, the result can be located, and unrelated work stays unchanged. What would you ask this artist before building anything?
topics.exercise: Write role, goal, benefit; add one observable success condition and one thing that must not change. Keep the full story-writing exercise for tool planning if peer preparation is already full.
topics.visual: A one-line story beside a short Maya → export → Unreal → inspect journey. Proposed course example, not a published studio workflow.

topics.title: Compare layouts before committing to one
topics.placement: Proposed insertion before 15; combine with grouping rather than adding a long software tutorial.
copy: Sketch two ways to support the same task
Show initial, result, and error states
Test what the artist thinks they can do
topics.example: For the same importer, compare a compact source/destination panel with a staged review flow. Neither is automatically better. Show where the artist would detect a wrong destination.
topics.notes: You can test an idea before writing the tool. Sketch two arrangements and ask a partner where they would start and what they expect next. Include a result and an error state; a single polished rectangle does not show the interaction. Paper is enough. Figma can connect these states into a clickable prototype. It still cannot prove that an Unreal import works. Which uncertainty could you test with a sketch?
topics.exercise: Instructor shows two rough alternatives and asks for a prediction. A full student sketch-and-test exercise needs a separate 3–5 minute allocation; it is not included in the proposed 20-minute route.
topics.visual: R1 Figure 1, PDF page 1, illustrates serial versus parallel process. F1 contains connected-frame illustrations. Link to originals; no open artwork license verified.

topics.title: Your mental model is not your user’s mental model
topics.example: An artist may expect an operation on one selected Actor to affect only that placement. If it changes a shared asset, the interface needs to communicate the wider scope.
topics.notes: You know how your code works. Your classmate brings a different picture of what the tool does, shaped by tools they already use. Before the action, ask what they expect to change. Afterward, compare that expectation with the result. Show the target and relevant state instead of requiring them to remember hidden context. Where might your tool’s behavior surprise another artist?
topics.exercise: Ask the tester to predict the affected objects before running the operation. Treat their explanation as evidence about expectations, not evidence that the implementation is correct.
topics.visual: P1 includes a mental-model cycle; use as a linked instructor reference. Pair with the existing renamer result, rather than adding an unrelated consumer UI.

topics.title: Help the artist act confidently
topics.placement: Weave into feedback and recovery slides; no separate Apple-history lecture.
copy: Use familiar behavior for familiar actions
Put routine feedback near the work
topics.example: An import summary can show changed, skipped, and failed items with paths. A consequential overwrite may need an explicit review step. Confirmations should not interrupt every harmless action.
topics.notes: Apple’s guidance gives us a useful question: does this information deserve to interrupt the person? Routine progress can stay beside the operation. A consequential action may need a clearer review. Familiar controls also carry expectations: if something looks like an ordinary selection list, people expect it to behave like one. In Unreal, start with conventions artists already know. What feedback needs their attention now?
topics.exercise: Contrast a routine completion message with a partial-failure report. Ask which needs a next action and why. Retain keyboard focus, readable labels, and noncolor cues from 15B.
topics.visual: A1 chapter links provide candidate video excerpts. G3 PDF pages 32–35 provide real tool-layout material. Prepare and inspect any chosen frame before placing it in the deck.

topics.title: Test throughout development; revise from evidence
topics.placement: Expand the existing peer-test transition rather than adding a detached testing lecture.
copy: Record the version and help given
topics.example: Observation: the tester opened the wrong destination. Interpretation: the destination label may be unclear. Proposed change: show the full target path. Retest: can a new tester select the intended target without help?
topics.notes: Feedback is most useful when it changes what we do next. Watch the task before asking for preferences. Record what happened, then separate your explanation from the observation. A sketch can test interpretation; a running tool can test the actual operation. After you change the tool, test again. In today’s three rounds, keep the version stable so you can compare observations; plan the revision and retest afterward. What evidence would persuade you that your fix worked?
topics.exercise: Use the same task across the three peer rounds. Record any emergency fix and changed version; do not treat results across versions as directly comparable. Three classmates provide useful leads, not proof that the tool is universally usable.
topics.visual: U5 has iterative-design diagrams. Link to the source; NN/g artwork permission is not implied by free reading access.
